history.action: route plan -> implement -> review -> qa (model, confidence 85)

acceptance.check: On a daily or every-other-day schedule a person created by hand, one schedule-linked transaction removes only the rows that transaction can be named for, and every other Upcoming row for that schedule is still listed. The count is exact and depends on where the payment lands, so both numbers are specified rather than one of them hedged: a payment dated ON the schedule's own next due date removes EXACTLY ONE row (that next due date); a payment dated on a LATER occurrence removes EXACTLY TWO rows — the schedule's next due date, which the schedule's own Paid badge consumes, plus the occurrence the payment was dated on. A payment that leaves the schedule's status not-Paid removes EXACTLY ONE row, the occurrence carrying its date. Two payments never remove more rows than that count times two.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Use 'View demo' on the setup screen, then Schedules -> Add schedule: frequency 'Days', interval 1, a payee and amount used by nothing else, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, starting today. Open the register and count the Upcoming rows carrying that payee; record the count and note each row's date — the schedule's next due date is the row dated today. Then add ONE transaction with that payee and amount dated TODAY. The count must drop by EXACTLY 1, and the row that disappears is today's. Today it drops by 3. Repeat the whole sequence with a transaction dated a LATER row (three or four days out): the count must drop by EXACTLY 2, and the two rows that disappear must be today's row and that later row — nothing else moves. Today it drops by 4. Add a SECOND payment on a different later occurrence: the count drops by exactly 1 more and the third row to disappear is that second occurrence. Today a second payment on a later occurrence removes three more. Repeat the whole sequence with frequency 'Every 2 days'; the same two counts (1, then 2) apply, where today they are 2 and 3.

acceptance.check: An unstamped transaction dated up to two days before an occurrence still discharges that occurrence, so the early-payment fallback keeps working: on a weekly manual schedule whose occurrences are Mondays, a transaction dated the Saturday before a Monday removes exactly that Monday's row and leaves every other row listed. This is identical before and after the change — it is a regression guard, and its status comes from the real status query for the fixture, not from a hard-coded value.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Schedules -> Add schedule: frequency 'Weeks', interval 1, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, starting on a Monday. Open the register and note every Upcoming row. Add one transaction with that schedule's payee and amount dated the SATURDAY BEFORE THE FOLLOWING MONDAY (two days early) — that is the row two occurrences down, not the next one. The rule links it unstamped. Exactly that Monday's row disappears; the schedule's own next-due-date row and the other Mondays are untouched. Then, separately, confirm the narrow direction: date a payment three days before a Monday instead and that Monday's row is still listed. Both of these are the behaviour today as well; this criterion exists so that narrowing the close-together overlap cannot quietly cost the early-payment fallback.

acceptance.check: A schedule whose date condition is an exact 'is' match, or which posts transactions automatically, behaves as it does now: an unstamped transaction discharges only the occurrence whose date it carries, and one dated a day earlier discharges none.
acceptance.how_to_verify: CI runs `yarn workspace @actual-app/core run test`. The cases are `a schedule with op is and an auto-posted daily schedule are unaffected` in packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.test.ts (named in tests[]), the existing `does not double-count daily recurring schedule occurrences with op is posted on the due date` in packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/app.test.ts, and the existing weekly `posting a specific occurrence` block in packages/loot-core/src/server/schedules/app.test.ts, whose `createWeeklySchedule()` fixture uses `posts_transaction: true` with `op: 'is'`. Add one transaction with that schedule's payee and amount dated the SUNDAY before the following Monday — the day before an occurrence. No Upcoming row moves. To be sure the transaction really was linked, check the schedule's rule has run (the transaction carries the schedule's category or appears in the schedule's Transactions list); an unlinked transaction would make this pass vacuously. acceptance.check: The forecast for a manual recurring daily schedule keeps an occurrence on the day after, and on the day after that, when a single transaction discharges only the first one. Today the forecast silently omits the following two occurrences and understates the projected balance.

alternatives_considered.approach: Drop the multi-day lookback from the preview path entirely and leave early-payment matching to the status query alone, as the issue offers as an alternative.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It satisfies IAC-1 by making the fallback window a single day, but it breaks IAC-2 outright: an unstamped payment up to two days early would no longer discharge the occurrence it was for, and the register would re-offer an occurrence that was already paid. That is the double-payment direction the issue names as the risk of over-narrowing.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep the rejected v1 step 4 — spend whichever transaction the coarse status query matched, using its lower-bound-only arm — and restate AC-2 to accept the re-offer as specified behaviour, promoting qa_script step 6 and the residual_risks entry from disclosure to specification.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is the branch the plan reviewer offered, but it makes an occurrence the user demonstrably paid for get offered again in the register. I ran v1's algorithm verbatim against AC-2's own scenario and it leaves 2017-01-09 listed while the head is dropped, so the Saturday payment discharges nothing at all. That is a product decision on a money path, and it should not be taken by default inside a bug fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Match occurrences to transactions (each occurrence takes the earliest eligible transaction) rather than each transaction to the earliest eligible occurrence.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It produces the same set of paid occurrences for every input I could construct, because the window `[occurrenceDate - 2, occurrenceDate]` is monotone in the occurrence date. The issue names the transaction-first direction, so that is what is specified; the implementer does not need to reason about the equivalence.

alternatives_considered.approach: Keep `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` and give it an extra parameter listing the occurrences already consumed.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: A per-occurrence predicate given a shared mutable 'already consumed' list is how the two callers would have to be kept in step by hand, and it leaves the caller responsible for the ordering. A function that takes the whole occurrence list and returns the paid set makes the one-to-one rule impossible to get wrong at a call site.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fix the preview path only, and file the forecast as a follow-up.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The forecast repeats the identical per-occurrence call over the identical list and has the identical defect, and the fix belongs in the shared module anyway. I measured it: on a manual daily schedule one transaction dated on the first occurrence makes today's forecast omit the following two days entirely. Leaving one caller knowingly broken is the outcome the planner rules single out. Flagged in `risks` so a human can overrule.

validated_work_order.approach:
Make the match one-to-one. Add `matchPostedScheduleOccurrences` to packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts: given a schedule, its id, the occurrence dates under consideration and the schedule's posted transactions, it returns the `Set<string>` of occurrence dates that are discharged, guaranteeing each transaction discharges at most one occurrence. `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` calls it instead of filtering with `isScheduleOccurrencePosted`, and hands it the coarse `status === 'paid'` claim as `paidByStatusDate`. `dates.shift()` stays exactly where it is — it is what drops the head when the posted-transaction list has not loaded yet, and it is what makes a payment dated AFTER the occurrence count as paid, which the two-sided comparison deliberately does not.

This is the revision of the rejected plan, and the change is in ONE step. v1 replayed `getHasTransactionsQuery`'s fallback arm (`schedule_occurrence == null AND date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, next_date)`, a LOWER BOUND ONLY) to decide which transaction the shift spent. Because that arm reaches arbitrarily far forward, it spent the very transaction the user made for a LATER occurrence, and the occurrence actually paid was re-offered. Step 4 is therefore narrowed to the head occurrence's TWO-SIDED window: a transaction is spent on the head only when `tx.date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, paidByStatusDate) && tx.date <= paidByStatusDate`, or when it is stamped for `paidByStatusDate`. A transaction outside that window is not spent, falls through to the unstamped pass, and discharges the occurrence it was actually paid for.

I ran this exact algorithm against the rejected plan's own AC-2 scenario and it passes: a weekly manual (`isapprox`, `posts_transaction: false`) schedule with occurrences 2017-01-02/-09/-16/-23/-30 and one unstamped schedule-linked transaction dated 2017-01-07 leaves [2017-01-16, 2017-01-23, 2017-01-30] — the Monday it was paid for is gone and the other three are listed. Under v1 it left [2017-01-09, ...], re-offering the paid Monday.

Because that narrowing changes how many rows move, AC-1 now states the count for each case explicitly instead of hedging about which row disappears. Measured on a daily manual schedule with occurrences 2017-01-02..2017-01-31 and one unstamped transaction:
- paid dated on next_date (2017-01-02), status 'paid': 1 row drops (next_date). Today 3.
- paid dated on a later occurrence (2017-01-06), status 'paid': 2 rows drop — next_date, removed by the coarse status bit, and 2017-01-06. Today 4.
- paid dated on any occurrence, status 'due': 1 row drops. Today 3.
Every-other-day behaves identically (1 / 2; today 2 / 3). Two payments on later occurrences drop 3 (head + both); today they drop 7.

Invariant for any input, asserted by a sweep in tests[]: the number of occurrences removed is never greater than the number of posted transactions carried for that schedule plus the one head the `dates.shift()` removes, and no occurrence is removed unless a distinct transaction can be named for it.

The matcher also runs in the forecast, which repeats the identical per-occurrence call over the same list. Verified there too: on a manual daily (`isapprox`, `posts_transaction: false`) schedule with occurrences 2024-03-10/-11/-12 and one transaction dated 2024-03-10, today's forecast keeps NONE of the three occurrences and the matcher keeps 03-11 and 03-12.
assumptions: `dates[0] === schedule.next_date` in `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` — it is built as `const dates = [schedule.next_date]` and only ever appended to, so `paidByStatusDate` is always a date the caller's list has just shifted off.

`statuses.get(schedule.id) === 'paid'` means `getHasTransactionsQuery` matched this schedule. Its fallback arm is a lower bound only, so the transaction it actually matched may be dated well after `next_date`. The plan deliberately does NOT replay that arm; it only claims a transaction that falls inside the head's two-sided window, which is a strict subset of what the query can match, so nothing the query matched is left unaccounted for except by the shift.

A QA user can reach the whole repro through the UI: the Schedules page's recurring picker offers 'Days' (desktop-client/src/components/select/RecurringSchedulePicker.tsx:38-43) and a schedule created there writes `posts_transaction: false` with an `isapprox` date condition, which is exactly the shape that takes the fallback arm. The `isapprox` date condition in `Condition` matches ±2 days around any occurrence (server/rules/condition.ts:281-287), so a transaction dated on an occurrence date is linked by the schedule's own rule and lands unstamped.
The register renders one Upcoming row per occurrence from `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions`, so the row count is the observable the acceptance criteria are written against.
validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: The defect was reproduced and measured against the shipped code (3 rows on a 'due' daily schedule, 4 on a 'paid' one, 2/3 on every-other-day, 7 for two later payments, and the forecast dropping two unpaid days). The revised algorithm was run as a prototype against every input that matters: the objection's AC-2 scenario now passes with the exact expected list, all seven existing weekly `OCCURRENCES` cases produce identical results, the AC-3 shapes (op `is`, `posts_transaction: true`) are unchanged, the AC-5 auto-post case removes nothing, and a sweep over every payment date of a daily schedule bounds the count at 1 per transaction plus at most 1 for the head. What remains uncertain is only the product judgement in `unknowns` — whether two rows is the right count for the behind-schedule case — which AC-1 now states explicitly so it can be overruled at the criterion rather than discovered at QA.

files.change:
Add ONE new exported function immediately after `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` (which ends at line 172), and no other new export:

export function matchPostedScheduleOccurrences({ schedule, scheduleId, occurrenceDates, postedTransactions, paidByStatusDate }: { schedule: ScheduleOccurrenceMatchInput; scheduleId: string; occurrenceDates: readonly string[]; postedTransactions: readonly PostedScheduleTransaction[]; paidByStatusDate?: string; }): Set<string>

Body, in this order:
1. `const ordered = [...occurrenceDates].sort();` — `yyyy-MM-dd` sorts lexicographically into chronological order.
2. `const paid = new Set<string>();`
3. Build `claimable`: `postedTransactions.map((tx, index) => ({ tx, index }))`, `.filter(entry => entry.tx.schedule === scheduleId)`, sorted by `tx.date` ascending and, for equal dates, by `index` ascending (`Array.prototype.sort` is stable and the input from `getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery` has no ORDER BY, so keep the explicit tie-break). Do NOT mutate `postedTransactions` — `claimable` is a fresh array and any removal below splices `claimable`.
4. `paidByStatusDate` spend — THIS IS THE STEP THAT CHANGED SINCE THE REJECTED PLAN, so implement it exactly as written and do not reintroduce the coarse form:
   `if (paidByStatusDate != null) {`
   `  const headStart = getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, paidByStatusDate);`
   `  const spentAt = claimable.findIndex(({ tx }) =>`
   `    (tx.schedule_occurrence != null && tx.schedule_occurrence === paidByStatusDate) ||`
   `    (tx.schedule_occurrence == null && tx.date >= headStart && tx.date <= paidByStatusDate),`
   `  );`
   `  if (spentAt !== -1) { claimable.splice(spentAt, 1); }`
   `}`
   The upper bound `tx.date <= paidByStatusDate` is the whole point and is not optional: it is what keeps a payment made for a LATER occurrence out of the head's claim, so that payment can discharge the occurrence it was actually made for. Remove the spent entry from `claimable` and do nothing else with it. Do NOT add `paidByStatusDate` to `paid` — the caller's `dates.shift()` already removed that row. If no entry qualifies, remove nothing: that is the case where the posted-transaction list has not loaded yet, and the shift must still fire on its own.
5. Stamped pass: for each `occurrenceDate` of `ordered`, if any entry of the remaining `claimable` has `tx.schedule_occurrence != null && tx.schedule_occurrence === occurrenceDate`, `paid.add(occurrenceDate)`. Two stamps naming the same occurrence still mark it once. A stamp naming a date outside `occurrenceDates` matches nothing.
6. Unstamped pass: for each entry of `claimable` whose `tx.schedule_occurrence == null`, in the sorted order, find the FIRST `occurrenceDate` of `ordered` that is not already in `paid` and satisfies `tx.date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, occurrenceDate) && tx.date <= occurrenceDate`; if one is found, `paid.add(occurrenceDate)`. Each entry is visited once, so it can claim at most one occurrence, and the `!paid.has(...)` guard stops it claiming one another entry already took. An unstamped transaction never claims an occurrence a stamp took, and a stamped transaction never takes part in this pass. This runs after step 4, so a transaction the head spent is already out of `claimable` and cannot also be handed to the next occurrence.
7. Return `paid`.

In `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions`, replace the `const unpaidDates = dates.filter(date => !isScheduleOccurrencePosted({...}))` expression at lines 594-604 with:

  const paidDates = matchPostedScheduleOccurrences({
    schedule,
    scheduleId: schedule.id,
    occurrenceDates: dates,
    postedTransactions: postedTransactionsBySchedule.get(schedule.id) ?? [],
    paidByStatusDate: status === 'paid' ? schedule.next_date : undefined,
  });
  const unpaidDates = dates.filter(date => !paidDates.has(date));

Leave the `if (status === 'paid') { dates.shift(); }` line at 580-582 exactly where it is, and leave `forceUpcoming`, the sort and everything else in the function alone.

Extend the comment block at lines 584-593 so it still explains why the two filters are deliberately not redundant, and adds, in the same voice: the shift is what fires when the posted-transaction list has not loaded, and it is what makes a payment dated after an occurrence count as paid; `paidByStatusDate` tells the matcher which transaction the shift already accounted for, so that same transaction is not also offered to the occurrence after it; and the matcher's two-sided comparison is what makes one transaction discharge at most one occurrence, so occurrences closer together than the 2-day lookback no longer overlap. Do not change `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate`, `getHasTransactionsQuery` or `getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery` — `getHasTransactionsQuery` in particular is load-bearing for `hasTransactionForSchedule` and `advanceSchedulesService`.

`isScheduleOccurrencePosted` KEEPS its export, its body and its doc comment. It is no longer called by either production caller, but it is the readable definition of the per-occurrence rule the matcher generalizes, `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate`'s doc comment (lines 83-89) points at it, and its existing test block is the executable specification of that rule. Deleting it is a separate cleanup and is listed in `out_of_scope` — do not do it here.

qa_script: Use 'View demo' on the setup screen, then create the fixture: Schedules -> Add schedule, frequency 'Days', interval 1, a payee used by nothing else, a distinctive amount, starting today, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF.
Go to the register and count the Upcoming rows carrying that payee. Record the count and each row's date; the row dated today is the schedule's next due date.
Add ONE transaction with that payee and amount dated TODAY. Count again. The difference must be EXACTLY 1 and the row that went must be today's. Today it is 3.

Undo that payment (delete the transaction), then add ONE dated a LATER occurrence (three or four days out). Count again. The difference must be EXACTLY 2 and the rows that went must be exactly today's and that later occurrence's. Today it is 4.
Add a SECOND payment on a different later occurrence. The count drops by exactly 1 more and the third row to go is that occurrence. Never 3 rows for one payment.
Repeat steps 2-5 with frequency 'Every 2 days'. The counts are 1 then 2; today they are 2 then 3.

Weekly schedule, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF: pay the SATURDAY BEFORE THE SECOND listed Monday and confirm exactly that Monday's row goes while today's row and the other Mondays stay. Then pay three days before a Monday and confirm that Monday's row is STILL listed.

Weekly schedule with 'Post transactions automatically' ON: pay the day before an occurrence, confirm the transaction is genuinely linked (it carries the schedule's category), and confirm no Upcoming row moves.

Regression sweep: a weekly auto-post schedule with two payments for two different occurrences still removes exactly those two rows; a non-recurring schedule's single Upcoming row still disappears when it is paid; re-dating a posted transaction off its occurrence date does NOT bring the row back.

Open Reports -> Forecast for an account with the daily schedule present and confirm the projected balance now carries an entry on the day after the paid occurrence and on the day after that. Before the fix those two days are missing from the projection.
residual_risks: A user who is behind on a daily schedule and pays an occurrence dated after `next_date` sees exactly two rows removed — `next_date` and the occurrence they paid — where today four are removed and the two occurrences in between are wrongly removed too. AC-1 states this count exactly rather than describing it as 'about one'. QA should exercise it and report what the register shows.

The change is a narrowing on a money path with no backfill: budgets whose unstamped transactions were being counted against several occurrences will see rows return. That is the intended correction but it is visible, and a user who believed a row had vanished because it was paid will now see it again.

The forecast change alters projected balances for close-together manual schedules. It corrects an understatement, but anyone who reconciled against the old (wrong) projection will see the number move.
risks: This narrows what counts as paid, on the path that decides which rows a user can still pay. The over-narrow direction is the dangerous one: a user who is behind and pays an occurrence dated AFTER `next_date` sees that occurrence's row listed again together with `next_date`'s — AC-1 specifies that as EXACTLY two rows rather than hiding it, because the schedule's own Paid badge is one bit about `next_date` alone and `getHasTransactionsQuery` reports it with a lower bound only. Today those same payments remove 4 rows; after the change, 2. The invariant 'one transaction discharges at most one occurrence' cannot hold together with 'a transaction dated after an occurrence still pays next_date' unless the transaction is attributed to `next_date`, which is what the plan does.

packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-schedules.ts is changed too, and no acceptance criterion on the issue covers it (AC-6 is about it, but the issue's IAC list does not mention the forecast). It changes forecast balances for budgets that have an unstamped schedule-linked transaction and occurrences less than 3 days apart: the forecast now includes occurrences it was silently dropping. That is a correction, but it is a visible change to a money number and a judgement call the ticket did not ask for. It is listed here so a human can strike it before implementation.

`isScheduleOccurrencePosted` is left exported with no production caller. `knip` is not run in CI (no workflow invokes it), so this will not fail a build; it is called out so a reviewer does not read it as an oversight.
The change is confined to `packages/loot-core/src/`; nothing under `forbidden_paths` is touched, no dependency is added, and no host outside `env.api_allowlist` is contacted.

`getHasTransactionsQuery` is deliberately NOT touched. It is load-bearing for `hasTransactionForSchedule` and `advanceSchedulesService`, where widening or narrowing it to later occurrences would change which occurrence a posted transaction marks paid and would move `next_date` for existing budgets. The two existing tests that pin it are at schedules.test.ts:381 and :412, plus the `compiles the fallback arm with AND, not OR` SQL assertion at :409.
validated_work_order.root_cause: The occurrence matcher is a per-occurrence predicate applied to an unbounded transaction list, so nothing stops one transaction from being counted for several occurrences. The overlap only bites when the gap between two occurrences is smaller than the 2-day lookback, which is why every shipped test missed it: `makeSchedule()` in schedules.test.ts uses `posts_transaction: true` and an `op: 'is'` date condition, both of which make `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` return the exact occurrence date and collapse the window to a single day. The fallback arm was never exercised through `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions`. The same defect exists one more time over in packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-schedules.ts:205-215, which calls the same predicate the same way over the same kind of list.

validated_work_order.understanding: The register's Upcoming rows for a schedule come from `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts:517). It builds the schedule's occurrence dates, applies `dates.shift()` when `status === 'paid'`, and then filters the rest with `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` called once per occurrence over the WHOLE posted-transaction list. For the schedule kind a person creates by hand (`posts_transaction: false`, date condition `isapprox` — ScheduleEditModal.tsx:76, schedule-edit-utils.ts:49), `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` returns `occurrenceDate - 2 days` and the fallback arm accepts any transaction dated in `[occurrenceDate - 2, occurrenceDate]`. That window is an interval, so when occurrences are closer together than the lookback it overlaps several occurrences at once: a daily or every-other-day schedule gets one payment counted against two or three occurrences. `link-schedule` (server/rules/action.ts) never writes `schedule_occurrence`, so every rule-matched transaction on a synced budget is unstamped and takes that fallback arm. I reproduced every number below by running the shipped `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` against real fixtures, and I ran the proposed matcher as a prototype over the same fixtures.
unknowns: Whether a maintainer wants the over-narrow direction to go further than this plan goes — that is, whether a user behind on a daily schedule who pays a later occurrence should ALSO keep seeing `next_date` offered (three rows for that state) instead of two. This plan keeps the `dates.shift()` because the comment block at schedules.ts:584-593 documents it as load-bearing and the existing test `does not let an unstamped transaction between occurrences un-pay any of them` depends on it. Both rows are stated explicitly in AC-1 so a human can see exactly what ships.

Whether the forecast correction should ship with this fix or separately. It is in `risks` for a human to strike; the plan takes the view that knowingly leaving one caller of a shared matcher broken is the worse outcome.
